text: The Tamil Nadu Legislative Council was the upper house of the former bicameral legislature of the Indian state of Tamil Nadu, initially established as the Madras Legislative Council in 1861 under the Indian Councils Act 1861 (24 & 25 Vict. c. 67), enacted after the Indian Rebellion of 1857. It began as an advisory body where the colonial governor could nominate four non-English Indian members, who could move and vote on bills but were not allowed to question the executive, examine the budget, or interfere with Central laws. The governor presided over the council and had full control over its convening, with only two members of his Executive Council and the Advocate-General permitted to participate. Most nominated members were zamindars and ryotwari landowners, with some, like G. N. Ganapathy Rao, Humayun Jah Bahadur, T. Rama Rao, and P. Chentsal Rao, serving for multiple terms. The council met infrequently, with a maximum of 18 sessions per year, and often convened at Udhagamandalam, which displeased Indian members. In 1892, the Indian Councils Act 1892 expanded the council’s role by increasing its members to a maximum of 20 (with no more than nine being officials), introducing a system of "recommendation" for elections by district boards, universities, and municipalities, and allowing members to discuss the annual financial statement and ask questions under limitations. Thirty-eight members were nominated during the eight elections from 1893 to 1909, including C. Jambulingam Mudaliar, N. Subba Rao Pantulu, P. Kesava Pillai, and C. Vijayaraghavachariar, though representation declined over time. The Indian Councils Act 1909 (Minto-Morley Reforms) introduced elected members, with 21 elected and 21 nominated, of which up to 16 could be officials and five non-officials, and allowed members to move resolutions on public interest and the budget. The Government of India Act 1919 enlarged the council, introduced dyarchy, and classified provincial subjects into reserved and transferred categories, with the governor retaining overriding powers over reserved subjects like law, finance, revenue, and home affairs. The council had a total of 127 members plus ex-officio members, with 98 elected from 61 constituencies—28 reserved for non-Brahmans—and 29 nominated, including up to 19 government officials, five representing marginalized communities, and one for backward tracts. The first election under this act was held in November 1920, with the first sitting on 12 January 1921. Five councils were formed in 1920, 1923, 1926, 1930, and 1934, with terms of three years (except the fourth, extended by a year), and control shifting between Justice Party majorities, fractured verdicts, and minority governments. The Government of India Act 1935 abolished dyarchy, created a bicameral legislature, and established a permanent Legislative Council with a minimum of 54 and maximum of 56 members, one-third retiring every three years, 46 elected directly, and 8 to 10 nominated by the governor. Members were classified into general and reserved categories, with a limited adult franchise based on property qualifications, qualifying roughly 7 million people (about 15% of Madras population). Two councils were formed in 1937 and 1946, both under Congress majorities. After India’s independence in 1947 and the adoption of the Indian Constitution in 1950, the council remained the upper chamber of Madras State, later renamed Tamil Nadu Legislative Council in 1968. It was a permanent body with a six-year term for members and one-third retiring every two years, with strength varying: 72 in 1952–53, 51 after Andhra’s formation in 1953, 50 in 1956, and 63 thereafter. The council could not pass laws independently and had to approve or disapprove those passed by the Assembly, with the Assembly’s will prevailing in case of conflict. The council was abolished on 1 November 1986 by the M. G. Ramachandran (MGR) administration of the AIADMK. MGR had nominated Vennira Aadai Nirmala (A. B. Shanthi), a woman declared insolvent, to the council; her nomination was challenged in the Madras High Court under Article 102-(1)(c) of the Constitution, but a lawyer, S. K. Sundaram, filed a public interest petition. MGR loaned her ₹4,65,000 to pay off debts, enabling her insolvency to be annulled under Section 31 of the Presidency Towns Insolvency Act 1909, which allowed retrospective annulment if all debts were paid. The judge, Ramalingam, set aside her insolvency, making the nomination valid, though Nirmala later withdrew it. The Governor, Sundar Lal Khurana, questioned MGR over the lack of proper vetting, causing embarrassment. Rumors circulated that M. Karunanidhi, then opposition leader, planned to enter the council to challenge MGR, prompting MGR to abolish the council permanently. On 14 May, a resolution to abolish the council was passed in the Legislative Assembly, and the Tamil Nadu Legislative Council (Abolition) Bill, 1986 was passed by both houses of Parliament and received presidential assent on 30 August 1986, coming into force on 1 November 1986. The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) has made three attempts to revive the council: in 1989–91, 1996–2001, and 2010. The 1989 and 1996 attempts failed due to lack of two-thirds majority in the Assembly and a friendly union government, with subsequent ADMK governments passing counter-resolutions. In 2010, the DMK, after winning the 2006 elections, moved to revive the council, with Governor Surjit Singh Barnala promising constitutional amendments. On 12 April 2010, the Assembly passed a resolution for revival. The Tamil Nadu Legislative Council Bill, 2010 was approved by the Indian cabinet on 4 May 2010 and passed by both houses of Parliament on 5 and 6 May 2010, receiving presidential assent on 18 May 2010 and being published the same day. Constituencies were identified in September 2010, electoral rolls prepared from October 2010 to January 2011, but in February 2011, the Supreme Court stayed the elections pending review of petitions. In the 2011 Assembly elections, the AIADMK, led by J. Jayalalithaa, won a sweeping majority and expressed no intention to revive the council, passing a counter-resolution to withdraw the revival attempt. Despite Article 168 of the Constitution providing for a Legislative Council in Tamil Nadu, there is currently no such body due to the absence of a majority resolution by the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly as required under Article 169. Fort St. George has historically been the seat of the Tamil Nadu government. Between 1921 and 1937, the Madras Legislative Council met within the fort. From 14 July 1937 to 21 December 1938, it met at the Senate House of the University of Madras, and from 27 January 1938 to 26 October 1939, in the Banqueting Hall (later Rajaji Hall) at the Government Estate on Mount Road. From 1946 to 1952, it returned to Fort St. George. In 1952, after the first legislative assembly was formed with 375 members, the assembly temporarily moved to the Government Estate complex due to seating limitations, then moved into a newly constructed building on 3 May 1952, later renamed Kalaivanar Arangam. After the reorganisation of states and the formation of Andhra in 1953, the strength dropped to 190, and the legislature moved back to Fort St. George in 1956, remaining there until January 2010. In 2004, during the 12th Assembly, the AIADMK government under J. Jayalalithaa attempted to shift the assembly (the council had been abolished) to Queen Mary’s College and later to Anna University campus, Guindy, but both attempts were withdrawn after public opposition.

The Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly initially rose to a strength of 375 after the constitution of the first legislative assembly and was briefly housed at the government estate complex in March 1952 due to the existing assembly building's seating capacity of only 260. On 3 May 1952, it moved into a newly constructed building within the same complex, which was later renamed Kalaivanar Arangam from 1952 to 1956. Following the reorganisation of states and the formation of Andhra, the assembly's strength reduced to 190, and it relocated back to Fort St. George in 1956. From December 1956 until January 2010, Fort St. George served as the legislature's home. In 2004, during the 12th assembly, the AIADMK government under J. Jayalalithaa attempted to shift the assembly—though the council had been abolished by then—to Queen Mary's College and later to the Anna University campus in Guindy; both plans were abandoned due to public opposition. During the 13th assembly, the DMK government led by M. Karunanidhi proposed shifting the assembly and government secretariat to a new building in the Omandurar Government Estate. In 2007, the German architectural firm GMP International won the design competition for the new assembly complex. Construction started in 2008 and was completed in 2010. The assembly operated in the new building from March 2010 to May 2011, after which it was moved back to Fort St. George in May 2011. During its existence as the upper chamber, the Tamil Nadu Legislative Council was used twice to appoint non-members as Chief Minister: in 1952, C. Rajagopalachari (Rajaji) was nominated by Governor Sri Prakasa to the Council to become chief minister, and in 1967, C. N. Annadurai became chief minister first before being elected to the Council. From 1861 to 1937, the presiding officer of the Madras Legislative Council was known as the "President of the Council"; from 1861 until dyarchy was introduced in 1921, the Governor of Madras also served as the President. After dyarchy, the first two presidents—Perungavalur Rajagopalachari and L. D. Swamikannu Pillai—were appointed by the Governor, while subsequent presidents were elected by the Council itself. From 1937 to 1986, the presiding officer was referred to as the "Chairman of the Council."
